generatedProse.concept-context: Different subjects use different referencing styles, with names like Harvard, APA, MHRA and Vancouver, and your department will tell you which one to use. Whatever the style, a reference is built from the same parts: the author, the date, the title, and where the work was published. Each style has its own rules for how these parts are punctuated and arranged. Once you can see the parts, a reference stops looking like a jumble and you can both read it and build your own.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students need to reference the same book chapter.

Student A copies a ready-made reference from the library's discovery service and pastes it in, then copies another from a PDF for the next source. The two are laid out differently, one puts the date in brackets and the other does not, and Student A does not notice. The parts are all there somewhere, but the list mixes styles and no single pattern holds.

Student B builds each reference from its parts: the author's surname and initial first, then the date, the title with the book title in italics, and the publication details, all in the one style the department asks for. Because Student B can see the parts, every reference follows the same pattern and a reader can scan the list with confidence.

Both students had the same sources. Only Student B recognised the parts and the style, and produced a reference list that holds together.
generatedProse.summary: Several referencing styles exist - Harvard, APA, MHRA, Vancouver and others - and different disciplines use different ones, so your department will tell you which to use. Underneath the differences, every reference is built from the same parts: author, date, title and publication details, arranged by the conventions of the style. You can now recognise the main styles, identify the parts of a reference, and say which style your own subject is likely to use. The next lesson is about using them accurately when you quote and paraphrase.

check.body: In the worked example, what let Student B produce a reference list that held together?

items.text: Building each reference from its parts and keeping to one style throughout.
Pasting ready-made references from the discovery service.
Using more sources than Student A did.
Choosing a different layout for each reference.

feedback.correct: That's right. Building each reference from its parts and keeping to one style made the list consistent.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B did that Student A did not.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B built each reference from its parts and kept to one style. Pasting ready-made references, piling up sources or mixing layouts all work against a consistent list.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
